title: Indian IT Stocks Plunge Up to 5% as Global AI Rally Resumes
excerpt: Infosys has shed about ₹25,000 crore in market value over two sessions as a rebound in the global AI trade, powered by SK Hynix earnings and Anthropic's IPO filing, extends the sell-off in Indian software services shares.
body:
• Indian IT shares fell for a second straight session on Wednesday, with Mphasis and Infosys down about 5% each and the Nifty IT index down more than 3%.
  • Infosys has lost roughly ₹25,000 crore in market capitalisation over the two days; TCS, Tech Mahindra, Coforge and HCLTech fell around 3% on Wednesday.
  • The trigger was a rebound in the global AI trade: SK Hynix profit rose more than seven-fold, Samsung gained nearly 9% and South Korea's Kospi rose 6%.
  • For investors: analysts are split between an AI-disruption risk to the traditional outsourcing model and an 'anti-AI' advantage for Indian services firms if AI spending disappoints.

Indian information technology stocks plunged on Wednesday, extending losses for a second consecutive session as a rebound in the global artificial intelligence trade weighed on software services shares. The Nifty IT index fell more than 3% to lead losses among sectoral indices, according to The Economic Times.

Mphasis and Infosys fell about 5% each. Tech Mahindra, Coforge, Tata Consultancy Services and HCLTech dropped around 3% each, while Persistent Systems, LTIMindtree, Wipro and OFSS fell about 1% each. The selling carried into the broader market in early trade, with the BSE Sensex down 500 points, or 0.7%, at 73,100 and the NSE Nifty down 114 points, or 0.5%, at 22,635, RTTNews reported. HCL Technologies, TCS, Tech Mahindra, Mphasis and Infosys fell 3% to 4% in that early session.

Across the two sessions, Infosys has shed about ₹25,000 crore in market capitalisation, making the Bengaluru-based company the most visible casualty of a rotation that is rewarding AI hardware and model developers while punishing the services firms investors fear could be displaced by the same technology.

Why the AI trade turned against Indian IT again

The immediate catalyst came from South Korea. SK Hynix shares surged more than 8% after the memory chipmaker reported a more than seven-fold increase in quarterly profit and announced plans to return about $75 billion to shareholders. The company forecast strong demand, supported by investment in AI infrastructure that has pushed up memory chip prices. Samsung Electronics advanced nearly 9%, and the Kospi, widely seen as a bellwether for the AI trade, soared 6%.

Wall Street had already risen on Tuesday as investors regained enthusiasm for AI-linked shares. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, filed for an initial public offering, a listing that would give public-market investors access to one of the leading developers of AI models. RTTNews also pointed to Meta Platforms' upsized $25 billion share sale, which ended five times oversubscribed, a $63 billion AI hardware deal announced by Broadcom, and Oracle's expanded partnerships with OpenAI and Nvidia.

The dynamic is not new for Indian IT. Anthropic's release of new plug-ins for Claude sparked a sharp rout in Indian IT shares earlier this year, as investors warned that AI tools could displace work now done by services firms. Traders at Jefferies dubbed the episode the 'SaaSpocalypse,' a sell-off in software-as-a-service shares, The Economic Times reported, citing Bloomberg. The shares later recovered some losses as analysts questioned the scale of AI spending and argued that India's IT sector holds an 'anti-AI' advantage. Renewed optimism in the AI trade has now reversed that recovery.

What lies ahead for the sector

Analysts remain divided on the direction of the trade. Michael Burry, the investor known for betting against the US housing market before the 2008 financial crisis, has warned of a potential market crash if the AI boom fizzles out. In that scenario, The Economic Times noted, Indian IT services firms could emerge among the key beneficiaries, because demand for conventional technology services would look more durable than valuations built on AI infrastructure spending.

The near-term test is whether the selling stays a sentiment-driven rotation or hardens into a reassessment of earnings. Indian IT companies earn a large share of revenue from clients in the United States and Europe, so any evidence that AI budgets are replacing, rather than adding to, traditional outsourcing contracts will matter more than a single session's price action. For now, the two-day fall has erased a large block of market value from the sector's biggest names, with Infosys alone down about ₹25,000 crore, and left investors waiting for company commentary and global AI earnings to decide whether the rebound in the AI trade has further to run at Indian IT's expense.
